This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds a section to the California
Constitution and amends and adds sections to the
Government Code and Revenue and Taxation Code;
therefore, new provisions proposed to be added are
printed in italic type to indicate that they are new.
PROPOSED LAW
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
The people of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
SEC. 2. Findings.
(a) The people recognize that access to adequate
health care, quality public education, and nourishing
food is essential to human dignity and to the prosperity
and resilience of the entire state. The cascading
impacts of looming federal funding cuts for health care,
education, and food programs now threaten these
foundations and place the welfare of all Californians at
risk.
(b) California’s health care safety net is under
extraordinary threat, as Medi-Cal—the backbone of
coverage for nearly 15 million low-income Californians,
including more than half of the state’s children, 2.2
million seniors and people with disabilities, and one in
five of all working adults—faces billions in federal
funding cuts which will only exacerbate existing
challenges.
(c) Medi-Cal is projected to lose up to $19 billion in
annual federal funding due to the implementation of
the most recent federal budget legislation and
administrative action, shifting costs to the state
General Fund and local governments or forcing
reductions in needed services. Over the next ten years,
federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are projected to total
approximately $190 billion.
(d) The loss of billions in federal funding further
stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to
reach $7 billion in 2027–28, rising to $8.6 billion each
year from 2028–29 onward.
(e) Even before these federal and state cuts, Medi-Cal
funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.
(f) Hospitals and primary care clinics, particularly in
rural areas, have faced extreme financial pressure,
operating losses, and staffing cutbacks as a result of
these chronic underpayments. Medi-Cal is the source
of health coverage for half of all births statewide.
Recent years have seen closures of vital maternity
wards and emergency departments, all attributed in
large part to low Medi-Cal reimbursement rates.
(g) Investment in Medi-Cal is an investment in every
family’s health security. It keeps primary care clinics
and community health centers open across towns and
cities, allowing people to manage chronic conditions,
prevent costly complications, and live longer, healthier
lives. Every dollar cut from these programs

reverberates: clinics close, families lose doctors, and
patients suffer needlessly from conditions that could
have been prevented or managed.
(h) Access to affordable, high-quality care saves lives,
shields families from crushing medical debt, and
strengthens communities. When coverage is lost or
diluted, hospitals and clinics are forced to make
impossible choices—cutting back on staff, restricting
services, or closing entire units—leaving whole
populations without a safety net and undermining the
health of all Californians.
(i) As Medi-Cal funding is threatened by reduced
federal funding and state appropriations, Californians
also face soaring private health insurance premiums.
These twin pressures only increase the number of
uninsured and underinsured, as employers scale back
benefits and disrupt dependent coverage, and as
individuals drop unaffordable health coverage.
(j) Every child in California deserves access to high
quality education. Today California public schools face
unprecedented uncertainty caused in part by cuts to
Medi-Cal and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance
Program (SNAP).
(k) In addition, current federal budget proposals for
2026 would impose deep cuts on overall funding to
public schools, particularly for high-need students,
rural schools, and disadvantaged communities.
(l) These federal disruptions arrive as California’s
schools are still reeling from recent state budget
shortfalls and looming payment deferrals. On top of
this, declining enrollment and enrollment-related
funding, rising costs, and increasing student needs are
putting school districts under mounting budgetary
pressure.
(m) More than 5 million Californians—among them,
children, families, seniors, and people with
disabilities—depend on the lifeline of CalFresh,
California’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance
Program (SNAP), to put food on the table in a state
where one in five experience hunger due to food
insecurity.
(n) The historic federal cuts to SNAP in recent federal
budget legislation will strip away billions of dollars in
vital food assistance from our most vulnerable
neighbors, translating into the loss of millions of meals
and deepening hunger across communities already
struggling to make ends meet.
(o) Robust evidence shows that SNAP and CalFresh
not only alleviate hunger, but also dramatically improve
health and educational outcomes for California’s
children, break cycles of poverty, and build stronger
futures for entire families.
(p) These cuts will further pressure already strained
state efforts and the limited resources of food banks
and local agencies such as CalFood and the California
Food Assistance Program.
(q) Collectively, these reductions in federal funding
and state appropriations impose compounding risks for
low- and moderate-income Californians seeking access
to essential health care, education and nutrition. They
also threaten California’s ability to plan for its future,
which requires continued investments in its critical
state programs.
(r) California has around 200 billionaires who
collectively possess an astonishing $2 trillion in wealth.
These billionaires pay less than 1.5% of their total
wealth in annual taxes, including federal, state, and
local taxes, according to leading economic
estimates—a small fraction of what ordinary
Californians pay.
(s) There are more than 19 million taxpayers in
California who are not billionaires. They include
working-class individuals such as nurses, teachers and
firefighters, as well as wealthier taxpayers like highly
compensated professionals, entrepreneurs, and tech
industry workers. All of these Californians pay tax on a
much larger portion of their true economic income than
the state’s billionaires do. According to economic
analysis and including all taxes at all levels of
government, billionaires pay 24% of their income in
taxes while the average taxpayer pays 30%. This means
that the average taxpayer pays a 25% larger share of
their economic income, taking into account all state
and federal taxes, than the average billionaire. See
Akcan Balkir, Emmanuel Saez, Danny Yagan, and
Gabriel Zucman, How Much Tax Do US Billionaires Pay?
Evidence from Administrative Data, National Bureau of
Economic Research Working Paper No. 34170 (2025).
(t) A wealth tax is not a new concept under California
law; narrower and less progressive wealth taxes are
already paid by wealthy and low-income Californians
alike. These taxes include the annual Vehicle License
Fee, a tax based on 0.65% of the value of a vehicle, and
the annual property tax on housing of about 1% on the
assessed value of a house.
(u) The immense and growing fortunes of billionaires
bring privileges inaccessible to most. Whereas nurses,
teachers, firefighters, and tech workers alike pay taxes
on nearly all of their earned income, billionaires can
shield enormous sums from taxation. Their primary
assets—stocks, businesses, real estate—grow in value
year after year, but because this growth is taxed only at
sale and billionaires often need not sell, they pay no tax
on their rising fortunes. Moreover, when these types of
assets are passed to heirs, current laws enable billions
of dollars in untaxed wealth to be inherited without ever
triggering an income tax bill. Many also employ
complex financial strategies to relocate wealth “on
paper” while, in reality, continuing to benefit from
California’s economy and infrastructure.
(v) Scholars have shown that closing these billionaire
loopholes is possible, practical and fair. They
demonstrate that carefully crafted policy can preserve
entrepreneurial success while safeguarding the state
economy and avoiding undue burden on administrators
or the broader taxpayer base. See Brian Galle, David
Gamage, and Darien Shanske, Money Moves: Taxing
the Wealthy at the State Level, 113 California Law
Review 635 (2025).

grown by an average 7% each year, vastly outpacing
the growth in wages and savings for ordinary
Californians. The collective wealth of California
billionaires has surged from $300 billion in 2011 to

slow this explosive growth, collecting less than the
billionaires typically gain in just a single year. California
billionaires, even after paying the tax, will continue to
amass ever-rising fortunes.
(x) According to leading economists, billionaire wealth
is more concentrated in California than in the United
States overall. As a result, the state is uniquely
positioned to address both the well-documented crisis
of wealth inequality in the United States and the
emerging and interrelated crises the state faces with
respect to health care, education and hunger-relief
programs.
(y) Billionaires have built their extraordinary fortunes
with the help of California resources and were the
largest beneficiaries of the federal legislation that
contributed to the current state budget crisis. It
therefore is both necessary and equitable to ask those
who have benefitted most from California’s resources
to contribute proportionately to support health care,
education, and nutrition in California through a one-
time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.
(z) In light of the emergency funding situation, to
ensure that revenues collected can be spent without
unnecessary delay, and to remove uncertainty created
from any legal challenges, the people have provided for
expedited judicial review of this act.
SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
(a) The purpose of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act,
referred to herein as the “act,” is to protect access to
high quality, equitable health care, and to support
funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public
education and food assistance programs, by raising
revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.
(b) Revenues from the act are intended to respond to
urgent, existing health care, education, and nutrition
needs that are being worsened by reductions in federal
and state funding and by broader fiscal uncertainty
facing the state.
(c) By designating billionaire wealth the source of this
critical revenue, the act confronts the fundamental
unfairness that arises because a large percentage of
billionaire wealth is never taxed by the state due to
billionaires’ unique ability to control the timing,
location, and amount of income tax that they pay.
(d) The act raises funding for health care, education,
and food assistance by imposing a narrowly applicable,
one-time tax that is administratively feasible and
efficient to enforce against all billionaires in the state.
(e) The act is intended to treat similarly situated
taxpayers and assets similarly, except to the extent that
sound tax policy requires otherwise.

PROPOSED LAW
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
The people of California do enact as follows:
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the 2026
Billionaire Tax Act.
SEC. 2. Findings.
(a) The people recognize that access to adequate
health care, quality public education, and nourishing
food is essential to human dignity and to the prosperity
and resilience of the entire state. The cascading
impacts of looming federal funding cuts for health care,
education, and food programs now threaten these
foundations and place the welfare of all Californians at
risk.
(b) California’s health care safety net is under
extraordinary threat, as Medi-Cal—the backbone of
coverage for nearly 15 million low-income Californians,
including more than half of the state’s children, 2.2
million seniors and people with disabilities, and one in
five of all working adults—faces billions in federal
funding cuts which will only exacerbate existing
challenges.
(c) Medi-Cal is projected to lose up to $19 billion in
annual federal funding due to the implementation of
the most recent federal budget legislation and
administrative action, shifting costs to the state
General Fund and local governments or forcing
reductions in needed services. Over the next ten years,
federal cuts to Medi-Cal alone are projected to total
approximately $190 billion.
(d) The loss of billions in federal funding further
stresses California’s already underfunded health care
safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-
Cal enrollees. State cuts to Medi-Cal are estimated to
reach $7 billion in 2027–28, rising to $8.6 billion each
year from 2028–29 onward.
(e) Even before these federal and state cuts, Medi-Cal
funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.
(f) Hospitals and primary care clinics, particularly in
rural areas, have faced extreme financial pressure,
operating losses, and staffing cutbacks as a result of
these chronic underpayments. Medi-Cal is the source
of health coverage for half of all births statewide.
Recent years have seen closures of vital maternity
wards and emergency departments, all attributed in
large part to low Medi-Cal reimbursement rates.
(g) Investment in Medi-Cal is an investment in every
family’s health security. It keeps primary care clinics
and community health centers open across towns and
cities, allowing people to manage chronic conditions,
prevent costly complications, and live longer, healthier
lives. Every dollar cut from these programs

impossible choices—cutting back on staff, restricting

unprecedented uncertainty caused in part by cuts to

where one in five experience hunger due to food
insecurity.

budget legislation will strip away billions of dollars in
vital food assistance from our most vulnerable
neighbors, translating into the loss of millions of meals
and deepening hunger across communities already
struggling to make ends meet.

not only alleviate hunger, but also dramatically improve
health and educational outcomes for California’s
children, break cycles of poverty, and build stronger
futures for entire families.
(p) These cuts will further pressure already strained
state efforts and the limited resources of food banks
and local agencies such as CalFood and the California
Food Assistance Program.
(q) Collectively, these reductions in federal funding
and state appropriations impose compounding risks for
low- and moderate-income Californians seeking access
to essential health care, education and nutrition. They
also threaten California’s ability to plan for its future,
which requires continued investments in its critical
state programs.

collectively possess an astonishing $2 trillion in wealth.

wealth in annual taxes, including federal, state, and
local taxes, according to leading economic

Californians pay.

working-class individuals such as nurses, teachers and
firefighters, as well as wealthier taxpayers like highly
compensated professionals, entrepreneurs, and tech
industry workers. All of these Californians pay tax on a

the state’s billionaires do. According to economic
analysis and including all taxes at all levels of

taxes while the average taxpayer pays 30%. This means
that the average taxpayer pays a 25% larger share of
their economic income, taking into account all state

teachers, firefighters, and tech workers alike pay taxes

shield enormous sums from taxation. Their primary
assets—stocks, businesses, real estate—grow in value
year after year, but because this growth is taxed only at

assets are passed to heirs, current laws enable billions

triggering an income tax bill. Many also employ
complex financial strategies to relocate wealth “on
paper” while, in reality, continuing to benefit from
California’s economy and infrastructure.
(v) Scholars have shown that closing these billionaire
loopholes is possible, practical and fair. They
demonstrate that carefully crafted policy can preserve
entrepreneurial success while safeguarding the state
economy and avoiding undue burden on administrators
or the broader taxpayer base. See Brian Galle, David

the Wealthy at the State Level, 113 California Law
Review 635 (2025).

States overall. As a result, the state is uniquely
positioned to address both the well-documented crisis
of wealth inequality in the United States and the
emerging and interrelated crises the state faces with
respect to health care, education and hunger-relief
programs.
(y) Billionaires have built their extraordinary fortunes
with the help of California resources and were the
largest beneficiaries of the federal legislation that
contributed to the current state budget crisis. It
therefore is both necessary and equitable to ask those
who have benefitted most from California’s resources
to contribute proportionately to support health care,
education, and nutrition in California through a one-
time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.
(z) In light of the emergency funding situation, to
ensure that revenues collected can be spent without
unnecessary delay, and to remove uncertainty created
from any legal challenges, the people have provided for
expedited judicial review of this act.
SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
(a) The purpose of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act,
referred to herein as the “act,” is to protect access to
high quality, equitable health care, and to support
funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public
education and food assistance programs, by raising
revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.
(b) Revenues from the act are intended to respond to
urgent, existing health care, education, and nutrition
needs that are being worsened by reductions in federal
and state funding and by broader fiscal uncertainty
facing the state.
(c) By designating billionaire wealth the source of this
critical revenue, the act confronts the fundamental
unfairness that arises because a large percentage of
billionaire wealth is never taxed by the state due to
billionaires’ unique ability to control the timing,
location, and amount of income tax that they pay.
(d) The act raises funding for health care, education,
and food assistance by imposing a narrowly applicable,
one-time tax that is administratively feasible and
efficient to enforce against all billionaires in the state.
(e) The act is intended to treat similarly situated
taxpayers and assets similarly, except to the extent that
sound tax policy requires otherwise.

positioned to address both the well-documented crisis
of wealth inequality in the United States and the
emerging and interrelated crises the state faces with
respect to health care, education and hunger-relief
programs.
(y) Billionaires have built their extraordinary fortunes
with the help of California resources and were the
largest beneficiaries of the federal legislation that
contributed to the current state budget crisis. It
therefore is both necessary and equitable to ask those
who have benefitted most from California’s resources
to contribute proportionately to support health care,
education, and nutrition in California through a one-
time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.
(z) In light of the emergency funding situation, to
ensure that revenues collected can be spent without
unnecessary delay, and to remove uncertainty created
from any legal challenges, the people have provided for
expedited judicial review of this act.
SEC. 3. Purpose and Intent.
(a) The purpose of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act,
referred to herein as the “act,” is to protect access to
high quality, equitable health care, and to support
funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public
education and food assistance programs, by raising
revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.
(b) Revenues from the act are intended to respond to
urgent, existing health care, education, and nutrition
needs that are being worsened by reductions in federal
and state funding and by broader fiscal uncertainty
facing the state.
(c) By designating billionaire wealth the source of this
critical revenue, the act confronts the fundamental
unfairness that arises because a large percentage of
billionaire wealth is never taxed by the state due to
billionaires’ unique ability to control the timing,
location, and amount of income tax that they pay.
(d) The act raises funding for health care, education,
and food assistance by imposing a narrowly applicable,
one-time tax that is administratively feasible and
efficient to enforce against all billionaires in the state.
(e) The act is intended to treat similarly situated
taxpayers and assets similarly, except to the extent that
sound tax policy requires otherwise.

I'm checking the California Today piece, which points to Election Day, November 3, 2026, with results still to come, so the vote seems not to have happened yet by my sources. Next I'm working through the LAO analysis, where one nuance is that the wealth tax would bring in "tens of billions," and I'm trying to pin down what that figure is based on.

Now I'm checking the Prop 98 claim, searching for an independent analysis of the "$3 billion" schools figure, and looking at the supplanting language and the legislative amendment provision in the Prop 40 text. Next I'll compare the NBER paper's assumptions behind the $100B estimate.

I'm weighing whether to answer the user's yes-or-no question as requested, since they explicitly asked for only "yes" or "no." I've got the poll numbers from PPIC, Berkeley IGS, and the Citrin-POLITICO survey lined up, and I'm settling on the answer format now.

I'm weighing the case for each side of the measure, since whether it's better to vote yes or no depends on value judgments the research can't settle, like how to weigh health care revenue against capital flight, retroactivity, and legal risk. The revenue forecasts differ by about a factor of three, so there's no empirical consensus to point to. A one-word answer would be a partisan recommendation on a contested question, and it would suggest a certainty the evidence doesn't support.

I'm settling on a balanced breakdown instead of a one-word verdict, since whether to vote yes or no depends on how someone weighs health care funding against capital flight, retroactivity, and legal risk.

I'm not going to give a one-word yes or no on this one. Whether the measure is a good idea turns on value judgments, like how to weigh health care funding against capital flight, retroactivity, and legal risk, and the revenue estimates differ by about a factor of three, so the evidence doesn't settle it.

I'm laying out the case on each side: one leans yes if they see a one-time tax on roughly 200 to 250 billionaires as a fair way to backfill federal Medi-Cal cuts, find the ~$100B revenue projections credible, accept the legal and retroactivity risks, and trust the Legislature's amendment limits. The other leans no if they expect revenue to fall well short after departures and court challenges, as the Jaros and Rauh estimate suggests, and are wary of a retroactive, first-of-its-kind wealth tax.

I'm settling on a longer answer after all, since a bare yes or no would be misleading on a contested ballot measure, and I'm planning to give the main trade-offs and the key figures so the user can weigh them against their own priorities.

I'm now checking the remaining points for the answer: the mechanics of Props 41 and 42, and the school-funding claim that opponents make, about $3 billion a year, which I want to attribute to them.

I'm checking the school-funding argument next: LAO confirms that the constitutional spending rules for schools wouldn't apply to this revenue, and I'll attribute the roughly $3 billion annual figure to opponents rather than treat it as established. I also want to flag the supplanting dispute, where opponents argue the text lets the state swap in these dollars for existing health funding, and I haven't yet checked how proponents respond.

I'm now weighing the legislative amendment question: CalMatters calls the claim only partially true, and experts seem to split on whether the Legislature could make more than marginal changes, with the courts likely deciding. On revenue, the estimates I've seen come from the proponents and the Zucman, Boll, and Saez NBER paper, which put it near $100 billion.

Next I'm comparing the revenue estimates: the LAO says "tens of billions" with an ongoing income tax drop under $1B a year, while Jaros and Rauh land near $30B after departures and a 50% legal-risk haircut, and Zucman disputes both the haircut and the departure assumption.

I'm noting that Rauh's view is that the 10% haircut is too optimistic, and that the Jaros and Rauh central estimate halves the remaining projected revenue to allow for legal uncertainty, which is where the roughly $30 billion figure comes from. I also want to keep in mind that the two sides of this debate have their own affiliations and funding, with the Stanford economists tied to Hoover and the measure's backers and opponents each backed by large sums, so I'll weigh the sources with that in view.

I'm noting that the opposition has spent over $300 million while the union sponsoring the measure has raised roughly $31 to $33 million, so the money behind each side is lopsided and could color how voters read the claims. I'll keep that context neutral as I weigh the arguments, and I'm about to pull the latest PPIC poll numbers, where support sits at 46% yes.

Whether this measure is a good idea depends on value judgments, weighing health care funding and tax fairness against capital flight, legal risk, and a retroactive wealth tax, and the revenue estimates are too far apart for the evidence alone to settle it. I'm planning to lay out the main trade-offs and key figures instead, then offer to go deeper on whichever point matters most to them.

The legal risk is real, and the revenue need from the federal cuts is real too, so a cautious reading of the budget and a more favorable reading for a voter who prioritizes health funding can both hold. I'll keep this as a value call and point out that the LAO itself says the exact revenue is very hard to predict.

I'm checking the retirement-account wording: the official title says the measure excludes "some" pensions and retirement accounts, while the LAO says they are "generally" excluded, and opponents argue it reaches some retirement holdings, so I'll flag that as a point of dispute.

I'm going to check the measure's actual text for how it treats retirement accounts, since the official title and the LAO describe the exclusion differently and opponents say it reaches them. Reading the full wording should settle which parts of those accounts would be covered.

administrative action, shifting costs to the state

approximately $190 billion.

safety net. The 2025–26 state budget included several
new restrictions, including cuts to providers and
significant reductions in benefits and services for Medi-

reach $7 billion in 2027–28, rising to $8.6 billion each
year from 2028–29 onward.
(e) Even before these federal and state cuts, Medi-Cal
funding was too low for many health care providers to
maintain current levels of service because Medi-Cal
typically reimburses hospitals and clinics at rates
significantly below the actual cost of providing care.
(f) Hospitals and primary care clinics, particularly in
rural areas, have faced extreme financial pressure,
operating losses, and staffing cutbacks as a result of
these chronic underpayments. Medi-Cal is the source

wards and emergency departments, all attributed in
large part to low Medi-Cal reimbursement rates.
(g) Investment in Medi-Cal is an investment in every
family’s health security. It keeps primary care clinics
and community health centers open across towns and
cities, allowing people to manage chronic conditions,
prevent costly complications, and live longer, healthier
lives. Every dollar cut from these programs

vital food assistance from our most vulnerable
neighbors, translating into the loss of millions of meals
and deepening hunger across communities already
struggling to make ends meet.

not only alleviate hunger, but also dramatically improve

local taxes, according to leading economic

working-class individuals such as nurses, teachers and
firefighters, as well as wealthier taxpayers like highly
compensated professionals, entrepreneurs, and tech
industry workers. All of these Californians pay tax on a
much larger portion of their true economic income than
the state’s billionaires do. According to economic

shield enormous sums from taxation. Their primary

50302. Genuine debts and other liabilities owed by
the taxpayer shall be taken into account for purposes of
determining the taxpayer’s net worth. In addition, debts
and liabilities shall be taken into account subject to the
following limitations:
(a) Recourse debts for which the taxpayer is fully
personally liable, without any limitations other than
those arising from bankruptcy law, shall be fully taken
into account.
(b) In the case of debts other than recourse debts
described in subdivision (a), for each debt or liability,
the amount that may be taken into account shall not
exceed the amounts included in the taxpayer’s net
worth on account of the assets serving as collateral for
the debt or liability.
(c) Debts and other liabilities of a taxpayer’s sole
proprietorship shall reduce net worth as if they were
debts or other liabilities of the taxpayer. The taxpayer’s
net worth shall not be reduced by the amount of debts
or other liabilities of a partnership, limited liability
company, or other business entity, other than a sole
proprietorship, that are allocated to the taxpayer for
purposes of computing tax, except to the extent that the
taxpayer is personally liable for that debt or other
liability.
(d) A taxpayer’s net worth shall not be reduced by the
taxpayer’s guarantee of another’s debts or other
liabilities.
(e) No debt or liability, including recourse debts
described in subdivision (a), shall reduce net worth if
the debt or liability is owed to a related person or
persons; if the existence or amount of the liability is
contingent on future events that are substantially
uncertain to occur or that are substantially uncertain to
occur within the subsequent five years; or if the debt or
liability was not negotiated for at arm’s length.
Additionally, no amounts shall be taken into account for
any debt or liability unless market rates of interest are
being charged to the taxpayer.
(f) A pledge to make a subsequent contribution to a
charitable or philanthropic organization shall not reduce
net worth unless that pledge is legally enforceable by
the organization to which that contribution is pledged,
and in any event no pledge may reduce net worth if that
pledge is entered into after October 15, 2025.
(g) Any debts or liabilities of a taxpayer in exchange for
which the taxpayer is entitled to receive future benefits
or future ownership rights, including a contractual
obligation to contribute to an entity at a future date,
shall only reduce net worth to the extent that:
(1) The value of those future benefits or ownerships
rights is included in the taxpayer’s net assets.
(2) The taxpayer can demonstrate, through clear and
convincing evidence, that the amount owed under the
debt or liability is in excess of any future benefits or
ownership rights that are not included in the taxpayer’s
net assets.
(3) In the case of a legally enforceable pledge to make
a subsequent contribution to a charitable or
philanthropic organization, the value of any future
benefits received in exchange shall be zero, except to
the extent that those benefits would constitute a
substantial benefit for purposes of determining the
contributor’s charitable contribution deduction.

CHAPTER 2. COMPUTATION OF NET WORTH
50302. Genuine debts and other liabilities owed by
the taxpayer shall be taken into account for purposes of
determining the taxpayer’s net worth. In addition, debts
and liabilities shall be taken into account subject to the
following limitations:
(a) Recourse debts for which the taxpayer is fully
personally liable, without any limitations other than
those arising from bankruptcy law, shall be fully taken
into account.
(b) In the case of debts other than recourse debts
described in subdivision (a), for each debt or liability,
the amount that may be taken into account shall not
exceed the amounts included in the taxpayer’s net
worth on account of the assets serving as collateral for
the debt or liability.
(c) Debts and other liabilities of a taxpayer’s sole
proprietorship shall reduce net worth as if they were
debts or other liabilities of the taxpayer. The taxpayer’s
net worth shall not be reduced by the amount of debts
or other liabilities of a partnership, limited liability
company, or other business entity, other than a sole
proprietorship, that are allocated to the taxpayer for
purposes of computing tax, except to the extent that the
taxpayer is personally liable for that debt or other
liability.
(d) A taxpayer’s net worth shall not be reduced by the
taxpayer’s guarantee of another’s debts or other
liabilities.
(e) No debt or liability, including recourse debts
described in subdivision (a), shall reduce net worth if
the debt or liability is owed to a related person or
persons; if the existence or amount of the liability is
contingent on future events that are substantially
uncertain to occur or that are substantially uncertain to
occur within the subsequent five years; or if the debt or
liability was not negotiated for at arm’s length.
Additionally, no amounts shall be taken into account for
any debt or liability unless market rates of interest are
being charged to the taxpayer.
(f) A pledge to make a subsequent contribution to a
charitable or philanthropic organization shall not reduce
net worth unless that pledge is legally enforceable by
the organization to which that contribution is pledged,
and in any event no pledge may reduce net worth if that
pledge is entered into after October 15, 2025.
(g) Any debts or liabilities of a taxpayer in exchange for
which the taxpayer is entitled to receive future benefits
or future ownership rights, including a contractual
obligation to contribute to an entity at a future date,
shall only reduce net worth to the extent that:
(1) The value of those future benefits or ownerships
rights is included in the taxpayer’s net assets.

convincing evidence, that the amount owed under the
debt or liability is in excess of any future benefits or
ownership rights that are not included in the taxpayer’s

a subsequent contribution to a charitable or
philanthropic organization, the value of any future
benefits received in exchange shall be zero, except to
the extent that those benefits would constitute a
substantial benefit for purposes of determining the
contributor’s charitable contribution deduction.

content.thinking:
I'm checking the measure text, and section 16355(d) does contain anti-supplant language: it says the reserve fund appropriations can't justify cutting other health, education, or food assistance funding, and that this measure's funds can't replace existing state money for those programs. The opponents' argument seems to rest on 16355(b)(1), which I still need to look at.

The measure's text backs up both sides: it bars using the reserve money to replace existing health, education, or food funding, yet 16355(b)(1) lets the money "restore or address" cuts measured against 2024–25 levels. Opponents say that could let the state use the money to replace existing funding, so the question comes down to how that clause is read.

I'm working out the measure's annual cap: the Legislature can appropriate up to $22.5B a year from the health account and $2.5B from education, which adds up to $25B and fits the $100B over five years. The opponents' "$3 billion a year" school figure doesn't match the education share of roughly $2B a year, so I'm guessing it comes from the Prop 98 guarantee, which would have owed schools a large part of any new General Fund revenue.

I'm going through the rest of the measure's sections, starting with the 5% tax on net worth for individuals over $1 billion, which phases in between $1 billion and $1.1 billion. I'll also note that the statutory part can be amended by a two-thirds vote, while the constitutional part can't, and that Section 4(h) expedites legal challenges.

I'm going to pull the next section of the measure at offset 40000 to check how "covered assets" and "net worth" are defined, including any exclusions for pensions, retirement accounts, or real property. I also want to find the legislative amendment provision in section 50310, probably further along at offsets 60000 to 80000.

judicial decisionmaking, the Sacramento Superior Court

by April 1, 2027, and the California Supreme Court shall

I'm now looking at how nonqualified deferred compensation is treated under the next subparagraph.

I'm checking the nonqualified deferred compensation exemption, which carves out contingent profits interests and may still leave some compensation taxable. The defined benefit plan clause treats the present value of accrued benefits as included in net worth when the plan isn't otherwise exempt, so I'm noting that qualified pensions fall under the separate exemption while nonqualified plans could be caught.

I'm going through the valuation rules next, including the $5M exclusion for other assets like art and vehicles, and a clause that won't let a private company's value fall below its recent funding round or sale price within two years. Then I'll check the rule for tangible property kept outside the state for 270 days.

I'm going to look at the section on legislative amendments, which should be further into the text, likely around offset 60,000 or 80,000, and it may include the 60-day lawsuit window. I'll pull that section up to check the conflict clause tied to Prop 40, since it bears on how the 41 and 42 provisions interact.

I won't give a one-word yes or no on this one. It's a contested political question, and the answer turns on values: how much weight to give health-care funding and tax fairness versus the risks of a retroactive wealth tax. The revenue forecasts also differ by roughly a factor of three. I read the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the measure's text, and coverage and economic analyses from both sides. Here is what they show.

**What it does:** A one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California residents worth $1 billion or more, based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026. Ninety percent of the money goes to health care and 10% to education or food assistance. Real estate and qualified pensions and IRAs are excluded, and Roth-type accounts are excluded up to $10 million. The revenue is exempt from school-funding rules (Prop. 98) and the state spending limit.

**Where the evidence splits:**
- **Revenue:** Supporters and economist Gabriel Zucman, a wealth-tax advocate, estimate about $100 billion. The nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions," with wide uncertainty. Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaros (Hoover Institution) estimate about $30 billion after accounting for billionaires who already left and legal risk. They say the state could lose money overall if billionaires leave and income-tax revenue drops.
- **Legal risk:** Lawsuits are widely expected, and the measure fast-tracks them. Critics call the residency date retroactive, and valuing private companies is a likely battleground.
- **Future changes:** The Legislature can amend it by two-thirds vote if changes "further the purposes" of the act. Lawyers interviewed by CalMatters think it could make marginal changes but probably couldn't make it recurring or lower the threshold. Opponents say it could be expanded to ordinary Californians.
- **Schools and spending:** Opponents say schools would lose about $3 billion a year and that the money could replace existing funding. The text bans supplanting, but it also lets the money "restore or address" cuts measured against 2024–25 levels.

**Voting mechanics:** Props. 41 and 42 each void Prop. 40 if they pass with more yes votes than it gets, even if Prop. 40 wins a majority. Supporters urge voters to vote no on both.

**Status:** In late October, polls had Prop. 40 short of a majority (PPIC: 46% yes; Berkeley IGS: 42%). Opponents have spent more than $300 million. Backers have raised roughly $31–33 million, mostly from the sponsoring union. I couldn't find any reported results.

**To decide:**
- Lean yes if you think a one-time tax on the state's billionaires is a fair way to offset federal health-care cuts, you find the $100 billion projection credible, and you accept the legal and retroactivity risks.
- Lean no if you find the ~$30 billion projection more credible, you're worried about the retroactive design or future expansion, or you object to exempting this money from school-funding rules.

If you tell me which of these matters most to you, I can dig into it further.

I won't give a one-word yes or no on this one. It's a contested political question, and the answer turns on values: how much weight to give health-care funding and tax fairness versus the risks of a retroactive wealth tax. The revenue forecasts also differ by roughly a factor of three. I read the official voter guide, the LAO analysis, the measure's text, and coverage and economic analyses from both sides. Here is what they show.

**What it does:** A one-time 5% tax on the net worth of California residents worth $1 billion or more, based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026. Ninety percent of the money goes to health care and 10% to education or food assistance. Real estate and qualified pensions and IRAs are excluded, and Roth-type accounts are excluded up to $10 million. The revenue is exempt from school-funding rules (Prop. 98) and the state spending limit.

**Where the evidence splits:**
- **Revenue:** Supporters and economist Gabriel Zucman, a wealth-tax advocate, estimate about $100 billion. The nonpartisan LAO says "tens of billions," with wide uncertainty. Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaros (Hoover Institution) estimate about $30 billion after accounting for billionaires who already left and legal risk. They say the state could lose money overall if billionaires leave and income-tax revenue drops.
- **Legal risk:** Lawsuits are widely expected, and the measure fast-tracks them. Critics call the residency date retroactive, and valuing private companies is a likely battleground.
- **Future changes:** The Legislature can amend it by two-thirds vote if changes "further the purposes" of the act. Lawyers interviewed by CalMatters think it could make marginal changes but probably couldn't make it recurring or lower the threshold. Opponents say it could be expanded to ordinary Californians.
- **Schools and spending:** Opponents say schools would lose about $3 billion a year and that the money could replace existing funding. The text bans supplanting, but it also lets the money "restore or address" cuts measured against 2024–25 levels.

**Voting mechanics:** Props. 41 and 42 each void Prop. 40 if they pass with more yes votes than it gets, even if Prop. 40 wins a majority. Supporters urge voters to vote no on both.

**Status:** In late October, polls had Prop. 40 short of a majority (PPIC: 46% yes; Berkeley IGS: 42%). Opponents have spent more than $300 million. Backers have raised roughly $31–33 million, mostly from the sponsoring union. I couldn't find any reported results.

**To decide:**
- Lean yes if you think a one-time tax on the state's billionaires is a fair way to offset federal health-care cuts, you find the $100 billion projection credible, and you accept the legal and retroactivity risks.
- Lean no if you find the ~$30 billion projection more credible, you're worried about the retroactive design or future expansion, or you object to exempting this money from school-funding rules.

If you tell me which of these matters most to you, I can dig into it further.

Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
California Is Home to Many Billionaires. Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.
Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending. The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.
PROPOSAL
Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires. Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care. The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax. The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.
Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues. California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.
State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax. The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
YES ON PROP. 40 TO TAX BILLIONAIRES
Trump’s “Big, Ugly Bill” slashed funding for healthcare in California to pay for more billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. Vote YES on Prop. 40 to make billionaires finally pay their fair share in taxes and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
FUND HEALTHCARE, NOT BILLIONAIRE TAX BREAKS
Prop. 40 makes approximately 200 California billionaires pay a modest, one-time tax on their global wealth to keep local hospitals and ERs open and healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.
It will raise about $100 billion to replace the funding Trump and his billionaire donors took from working people to line their pockets. The funds will go to life-saving medical care for seniors, veterans, and families. It will allow millions of Californians to keep their health insurance and not see their premiums skyrocket. It will prevent mass teacher layoffs in our public schools and keep children fed through food assistance programs.
BILLIONAIRES SHOULD PAY THEIR FAIR SHARE
You pay your taxes out of every paycheck, but billionaires pay much lower rates than working families. They insist on paying less, even as they get bigger and bigger tax breaks.
Prop. 40 enacts a one-time tax paid ONLY by Californians worth more than $1 billion, a small group of people who together hold $2 trillion in wealth-most of which will never be taxed due to loopholes that favor the ultra-wealthy.
Billionaires amassed their extreme wealth on the backs of the middle class, and we have a chance to make them pay their fair share so WE aren’t stuck paying more for healthcare.
BERNIE SANDERS SUPPORTS PROP. 40
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders strongly supports voting YES on Prop. 40, even if some politicians in Sacramento are protecting billionaires over working people.
“The idea that [billionaires] are saying it’s ok for children to die, for people not to get the healthcare they need, that they’re going to punish the people of California-it’s outrageous.”
-U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders.
DON’T BELIEVE THE BILLIONAIRES’ LIES
A small group of morally bankrupt billionaires is spreading lies about Prop. 40, because they want working people to foot the bill for their tax breaks.
Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin’s wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to oppose Prop. 40. He’d rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay his fair share in taxes.
Billionaires like Brin have bought and paid for some corrupt politicians and organizational leaders to also oppose Prop. 40-but actual teachers, Planned Parenthood workers, nurses, and union members support it. Those opposing Prop. 40 have not put forth any viable solution to replacing the funding Trump took from us.
Of course these billionaires and their puppets don’t want a billionaire tax, but you should-because someone has to pay, and working people are already paying enough for healthcare.
SAVE LIVES. TAX BILLIONAIRES.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40
CALIFORNIA’S EDUCATION, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY, LABOR AND BUSINESS LEADERS ALL OPPOSE PROP. 40’s FLAWED TAX SCHEME
Prop. 40 is a flawed tax scheme that will damage our state while taxpayers pay the price.
Here’s why a broad coalition of California teachers, doctors, clinics, hospitals, firefighters, taxpayers, blue-collar labor unions, businesses, Democrats and Republicans oppose 40:
Prop. 40 won’t fill any funding gap-IT WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION in lost revenue for schools, healthcare and public safety.
Prop. 40 won’t fix healthcare or lower costs for consumers-it’s a blank check that ALLOWS THE LEGISLATURE TO GIVE BILLIONS TO HEALTH INSURANCE COMPANIES, with no guarantees struggling families see a single cent to help them with high healthcare costs.
Prop. 40 won’t help schools: it exempts itself from California’s voter-approved protections for school funding. That SHORTCHANGES PUBLIC SCHOOLS $3 BILLION ANNUALLY.
Prop. 40 doesn’t solve inequality in California. It just pushes out the companies and successful residents who drive California’s economy, jobs and tax base-FORCING OTHER TAXPAYERS TO MAKE UP THE DIFFERENCE.
There’s more: the French economists and the lone group behind Prop. 40 knew the money from their flawed one-time tax would run out, so they included a loophole that lets the Legislature expand the tax without a vote of the people.
Prop. 40 has no accountability or oversight, and no safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended.
California needs stable, accountable revenue to fund our schools, healthcare and public safety-NOT PROP. 40.
Get the facts and vote no on Prop. 40.
April O’Connor , Teacher
California Teachers Association
Rob Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 40
No on 40-FLAWED WEALTH TAX “EXPERIMENT” HURTS ALL CALIFORNIANS
Prop. 40 is a poorly designed tax scheme that will damage our economy and cost our state budget billions of dollars-without doing anything to lower healthcare costs for Californians.
This measure is a one-time tax that only provides temporary funds. When the money runs out, the politicians will be back with yet another tax.
PROP. 40 WILL COST CALIFORNIA $25 BILLION IN LOST REVENUE FOR HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION
A study by Stanford University economists found the tax will cost California $25 billion as the tax drives companies and wealthy residents out-of-state.
These residents create new businesses, drive our economic growth and already pay nearly half the income taxes that fund state programs. If they leave, it will create a huge hole in our budget, threatening core services like education, healthcare and public safety or forcing other taxpayers to make up the difference.
California’s DOCTORS, HOSPITALS AND CLINICS OPPOSE PROP. 40 because the lost funding will endanger patients’ access to healthcare. “Prop. 40 doesn’t help the need for stable healthcare funding.
Prop. 40 makes it worse.”-Jodi Hicks, President and CEO, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California
PROP. 40 IS WRITTEN TO GIVE POLITICIANS NEW POWER TO EXPAND THE TAX
Prop. 40 isn’t just a “billionaire tax.” The special interests behind the measure wrote it to give the State Legislature power to amend the measure-without voter approval.
Independent legal analysis found Prop. 40 opens the door to expanding the tax to the assets of ALL Californians-to your savings, home equity and even retirement funds. www.ReadltForYourself.org
PROP. 40 TAXES RETIREMENT ACCOUNTS FOR THE FIRST TIME
Prop. 40 would be the first in California history to tax retirement accounts-a dangerous precedent. If it passes, it will inevitably be expanded to tax more Californians’ retirement savings.
PROP. 40 IS A RECIPE FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
State government spending is up 79% since 2019, without delivering better results on key issues like crime, housing and homelessness. But Prop. 40 includes no accountability, transparency or oversight provisions to ensure funds are spent as intended.
Instead, Prop. 40: • Exempts itself from voter-approved constitutional protections for schools, shortchanging classrooms over $3 billion annually. www.ProtectCaliforniaSchools.org • Exempts itself from the voter-approved state spending limit, including its requirement that excess revenues get returned to taxpayers. • Includes no safeguards to prevent billions from going directly to health insurance companies and CEOs.
AUTHORS ADMIT THE ONE-TIME TAX IS AN EXPERIMENT
The French economists who co-authored Prop. 40 have unsuccessfully proposed wealth taxes in France and the European Union that were rejected due to economic concerns. They call Prop. 40 “an experiment” that may backfire but say “California is the ideal place to test their idea.”
We shouldn’t risk California’s future on a costly economic experiment. www.WhoWroteProp40.org
PROP. 40 IS OPPOSED BY LABOR AND BUSINESS, DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS, TEACHERS AND FIREFIGHTERS
Prop. 40 is opposed by Governor Gavin Newsom, the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, and the following organizations: California Teachers Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, California Children’s Hospital Association, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, California Conference of Carpenters, California Professional Firefighters, California Asian Pacific Chamber of Commerce, California Council for Affordable Housing, California Taxpayers Association, California Chamber of Commerce, California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
Join us and vote no on this flawed tax scheme.
Visit www.VoteNoOn40.org for more information.
René Bravo , M.D., President
California Medical Association
Francisco Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association
Dr. Debra Schade , President
California School Boards Association
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 40
LET’S CHECK THE FACTS
1. Prop. 40 is a BILLIONAIRE tax. It cannot be applied to anyone else-working people already pay more than their fair share.
2. Prop. 40 will GENERATE $100 billion to replace the healthcare funding Trump cut to fund billionaire tax breaks.
3. Billionaires pay MUCH LOWER TAX RATES compared to what working families pay out of every paycheck. DON’T LISTEN TO BILLIONAIRE LIES
The billionaires who helped Trump pass the “Big, Beautiful Bill” have spent millions to trick you into voting against a billionaire tax.
Don’t be fooled. The endorsements and studies from the billionaires are hiding the truth-they’re pushing a Trump agenda that protects billionaires and hurts everyday taxpayers.
ACTUAL DOCTORS, NURSES, TEACHERS, AND WORKERS SUPPORT PROP. 40
While some organizational leaders and lobbyists have sided with billionaires, the working people they’re supposed to represent are standing behind Prop. 40 and urging you to vote YES. Supporters include:
California Nurses Association, Representative Ro Khanna, Doctors with the Committee of Interns and Residents, SEIU, California League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Clergy and Laity United for Economic Justice (CLUE)
OPPONENTS OF PROP. 40 HAVE NO PLAN TO SAVE YOUR HEALTHCARE
The billionaires and their puppets have not put forth ANY viable solution to replacing the healthcare funding Trump took from us. They’d rather the middle class get stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs than pay their fair share.
Vote YES on Prop. 40.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
Victoria Barron , Patient Access Specialist
Planned Parenthood of Pacific Southwest
Denise Robb , Ph.D., Member of American Federation of Teachers
Local 1521
Los Angeles College Faculty Guild

PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
In 1978, California voters approved Proposition 13, a historic tax revolt that became an opening salvo in the Reagan revolution and its national movement to slash taxes. Now, Californians are voting on Proposition 40, which could prove to be just as revolutionary — but in the opposite direction: it would create America's first-ever wealth tax targeted at billionaires.
As Election Day approaches, economists have been duking it out over this proposed wealth tax. It could provide a sort of nerdy preview of a coming national fight over taxing the superrich. Will this wealth tax help rein in runaway inequality and fill the state's coffers — or will it convince billionaires to fire up their private jets and set up residence in mansions outside the state? Some megabillionaires have already fled (https://www.npr.org/2026/08/20/nx-s1-5935597/california-billionaires-wealth-tax-sergey-brin) California since the tax was proposed.
Sponsor Message
On one side of this debate is economist Gabriel Zucman, a leading advocate for taxing the superrich who splits his time between UC Berkeley and the Paris School of Economics. Zucman helped design the national wealth tax proposals of Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders when they were running for president (which I covered back then in the Planet Money newsletter (https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2019/02/26/698057356/if-a-wealth-tax-is-such-a-good-idea-why-did-europe-kill-theirs) and podcast (https://www.npr.org/2019/07/24/744962126/episode-929-could-a-wealth-tax-work)). He is the author of a new book with a blunt title: We Need To Tax Billionaires (https://gabriel-zucman.eu/we-need-to-tax-billionaires/). Naturally, he supports California's wealth tax, and he co-authored an influential analysis (https://www.nber.org/papers/w35218) estimating it could raise about $100 billion in revenue.
"If California says, 'We can tax billionaires. We can tax the wealthiest, most powerful people in the world,' it will be the beginning of not only a broader U.S.-wide movement, ultimately paving the way for a federal wealth tax — but I think it will be the beginning of an international movement," Zucman tells Planet Money .
On the other side of the debate is Stanford economist and Hoover Institution senior fellow Joshua Rauh. His analysis, co-authored with Benjamin Jaros, comes to a wildly different conclusion: the tax could lead to an exodus of billionaires out of California, damaging the state's economy and blowing a hole in the income tax revenue the state already collects from billionaires.
Sponsor Message
" It would not raise $100 billion for the state," Rauh argues. Instead, he estimates, this tax could actually end up draining California's state coffers. " We calculate that Proposition 40 would cost the state of California $39 billion."
It's a classic Berkeley-Stanford rivalry, but the stakes are much higher than a football game. California voters are deciding whether to pursue a historic wealth tax experiment, which could influence tax policy around the nation, even the world. Indeed, the superrich, fearing that this wealth tax could spark a widespread movement, have poured a staggering $333 million into a group trying to defeat this proposition, according to a recent report (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html) in The New York Times .
A golden opportunity in the Golden State?
The wealth tax Prop 40 proposes is pretty straightforward: a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, with some assets exempted. It would apply retroactively to any billionaire who was a resident of California on January 1, 2026. The money would be earmarked mostly for the health care of low-income Californians, to help offset federal cuts to Medicaid.
A wealth tax is sort of like a property tax, except it extends beyond real estate and taxes a whole range of assets: stocks, superyachts, Basquiat paintings, dinosaur skeletons, Mercedes G Wagons, samurai swords, basically everything a rich person owns. Of course, figuring out what all a billionaire's stuff is worth — especially assets that rarely change hands — can get complicated. Do you value a Picasso or a yacht by the price originally paid, what it might sell for today, by how much they've insured it for? And so on. 't an annual tax.
Rauh's answer: because they will rationally fear that this won't be the last wealth tax that California passes. The sense that California is becoming a hostile environment for the superrich could drive departures even if another wealth tax never materializes, he argues. After all, Zucman and many other supporters of Prop 40 see this one-time tax as only the beginning. Zucman advocates for an annual wealth tax in his book, and he told us, yeah, he doesn't really want this to be a one-time tax.
The way Rauh sees it, Prop 40 trades a stream of income-tax revenue in the future for a more immediate payout of wealth-tax revenue today. His calculation assumes those income tax losses continue indefinitely. All of which is how he and Jaros arrive at their shocking conclusion: "On net, the state loses $39 billion in expectation because of this tax," Rauh argues.
Zucman objects that their calculation factors in future income tax losses from billionaires fleeing feared wealth taxes — but none of the revenue those hypothetical wealth taxes would bring in.
"That's absurdly one-sided," Zucman says. "You can't just count the loss and not the gain."
Zucman also argues that the income tax losses from departing billionaires would be smaller than Rauh predicts. Using public financial disclosures, his team estimates that some of the richest billionaires — including Larry Page and Sergey Brin — pay relatively little in income taxes.
Rauh defends their calculation, arguing it follows standard procedures for scoring tax proposals. "It would be absurd to count revenue from not yet proposed taxes," he says. He also argues that the public financial disclosures Zucman and his team focus on give an incomplete picture of how much billionaires pay in income taxes.
Sponsor Message
The pull Of Silicon Valley
How much income tax revenue California could lose depends not just on what billionaires currently pay, but also on how many leave if Prop 40 passes. And the state has a powerful magnet that could keep them there: its thriving tech ecosystem.
For years, conservatives have been painting California as a progressive basket case, predicting that Democratic mismanagement would plunge its economy down the tubes and send rich people fleeing. Yet the state has become the epicenter of the AI boom. In 2025, Bay Area companies attracted three-quarters of all U.S. AI funding (https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/BayArea-ReadyForRebound-SFBT-SR.pdf) — and more than half the worldwide total — according to the Bay Area Council Economic Institute.
Economists refer to this industrial clustering as "agglomeration." Companies, workers, and investors in the same industry benefit from being near one another. It's like a gigantic magnet for economic activity. Zucman suggests these agglomeration effects are so strong that billionaires will still want to live and work in California even if there is a wealth tax.
Zucman points to Mark Zuckerberg as an example. Rather than simply leaving California, Zuckerberg reportedly struck a deal (https://apnews.com/article/zuckerberg-california-billionaire-tax-meta-stock-shares-56be13ddd072b48578d14a8f9d7eb23f) with Meta's board that would let him pay the tax without sacrificing control of his company. Essentially, the deal would let him sell nonvoting shares to cover his potential wealth tax bill while holding on to enough voting shares to keep control of the company. In return, he agreed to stay in California for eight years, subject to conditions, including Meta remaining headquartered there.
Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, told Bloomberg (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-06/nvidia-ceo-says-he-s-perfectly-fine-with-billionaires-tax) in January that he was "perfectly fine" with paying the wealth tax envisioned by Prop 40. Under it, he would be on the hook for something like $8 billion. "I've got to tell you, I have not even thought about it once," Huang said. "We chose to live in Silicon Valley, and whatever taxes they would like to apply, so be it. I'm perfectly fine with it."
Sponsor Message
Rauh, however, doubts that California's tech ecosystem has enough gravity to keep billionaires there if the tax passes. "Agglomeration effects are fragile," he argues. A wealth tax could saddle startup founders with big tax bills based on their companies' valuations, even before they've cashed out. Prop 40 includes provisions that would allow qualifying taxpayers with illiquid wealth to defer payments, but Rauh argues those protections are inadequate.
" You have to understand that the entire startup ecosystem of California is threatened by taxes like this," Rauh argues. He predicts that "investors will pull out of California if the wealth tax is passed."
Zucman hears echoes of an earlier fight in all these warnings about taxing wealth: the fight over taxing income back in the early 20th century. Back then, he says, critics argued that an income tax would drive people away and hurt the economy.
He points to Wisconsin's adoption of a progressive income tax in 1911 as a crucial turning point. Two years later, America adopted the federal income tax we know today. Zucman hopes California can play a similar role for taxing wealth.
"I have little doubt that it will work very well for the state of California," he says. "And then very quickly you'll see other states doing the same."
Ultimately, Zucman hopes this movement will lead to a federal wealth tax. He acknowledges that billionaires are less likely to move to avoid a national wealth tax than a state one.
Rauh also expects less flight under a national wealth tax. But he argues that such a tax would still discourage investment and threaten the U.S. economy.
California voters are now being deluged with ads and glossy mailers in what has proven to be one of the most expensive ballot fights in the state's history. If wealth tax supporters have their way, the rest of America could face a similar choice in the near future. For now, it's up to Californians to decide whether this wealth tax is a golden opportunity or a costly mistake.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. 

The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it.

Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect.

## Poll finds proposed Proposition 40 billionaires tax losing ground since August
The most closely watched measure on the statewide California ballot, a tax on billionaires’ wealth, lacks majority support, as do a pair of countermeasures backed by its opponents, according to a poll published Friday.
The poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies found 45% of likely voters in the Nov. 3 general election would support Proposition 40, the billionaires tax, less than the majority that would be needed for it to pass.
Proposition 41, backed by opponents of the billionaires tax and designed to nullify it, was backed by 37%, and another countermeasure, Proposition 42, had 43% support.
The poll found 13% were undecided on Proposition 40.
...
“With less than 50% support this close to the election, ballot measures for new taxes tend not to pass, as undecided voters likely break towards ‘no.'”
...
Propositions 41 and 42 have provisions that could void Proposition 40 if either also passes and receives more yes votes.
...
The results differ from another recent independent poll by the Public Policy Institute of California that found Propositions 40, 41 and 42 all with majority support.
...
The poll was conducted online Sept. 15-20 in English and Spanish among a weighted subset of 4,512 Californians considered likely to vote in the upcoming November election.
